chunks.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I'm here at St. Ebbs Church with not only one of my favorite, no, no, my favorite apologist, but also one of my favorite people of all time, the esteemed wonderful Dr. John Lennox. Dr. Lennox, I can't tell you how good it is to see you after, it must be 15 years since we were in the presence of one another. You came to our house in Charlotte many years ago, and that was one of the highlights of my life to have you and Sally over our house for dinner for New Year's Eve. It was wonderful. Well, we enjoyed that, Frank. I remember it so clearly and well when I've forgotten many things. We've had such good experience in life with our friends in the U.S., so it's lovely to welcome you here to Oxford. We're at St. Ebbs Church right here in Oxford, where you've taught here for how many years at Oxford, John? Well, I've been here around 30 years. I came in 1997. So almost 30 years. I haven't taught all that time, but I've been teaching all my life, so. Now, your new autobiography is such a splendid tome. It's almost 700 pages, but it reads like it's about 100. I breezed right through it. It is so well done. It's a spiritual and intellectual journey. And I don't know how you remember all these places you've been, John. I mean, you've been all over the world. You've spoken to audiences about Christ in five different languages. You've been behind the Iron Curtain. You've been to Russia so many times. You've been to Ukraine. You've been down under. And the book is just so well done. How did you, how were you able to pull all these details together? I don't really know. I think part of it is that when I was traveling behind the Iron Curtain, we had a group of us that formed a trust. And so we had to have, by law, trust meetings and reports. And that helped enormously. Also, I'd written various reports through the years, but unfortunately, I didn't think very much of what was happening in the sense that I didn't realize how historic it was. So I didn't keep as accurate a diary. In fact, I hardly kept a diary at all. But there was enough evidence out there that I was able to scrape from talks, reports, all this kind of thing. And it came together in the end pretty well. And I had several friends who had accompanied me on these journeys and whose memories were better than mine. So I used other people's memories and even details in odd diaries of flights and ticket stubs. Oh, I went to there at this time. But it seems to have come together fairly well. Very well. And I want to sort of start at the end. I'm a big believer, Dr. Lennox, that we ought to know what the purpose of life is so we can live it well. And you gave a talk, I think it may have been at Florida State. And let me get the exact name of the talk. This is the name of the talk that you gave. And I want to ask you to sort of summarize what you said here. The talk was called Why Are We Here? God, Life, and the Pursuit of Happiness. Why are we here? Well, I believe we're here because this is a created universe by an intelligent creator. And we have been made in his image, which is hugely important. We have been created with consciousness. And we've got five senses. And it is through those senses that we apprehend what's around us, and they mediate meaning. We see things. We perceive beauty. We hear things. We can understand language because God has made us as talking people. So for me, it centers around the dignity of being a created being, but not simply a created being, created in the image of a personal God. By that, I mean that the universe, and I have been an amateur astronomer. I love looking at the galaxies and all the rest of it. They show the glory of God, but they were not made in his image. Human beings were. And I think at a time when people, particularly young people, are searching for meaning and purpose and all the rest of it, if we leave the creator out of the equation, I'm afraid we end up in darkness and confusion and meaninglessness. So I find it very important to start where the Bible starts. That's in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. And what it does, actually, that statement, and God created men and women in his own image, that actually represents the foundation of any value system that's worth talking about. I remember listening to Jordan Peterson reading Genesis, and he came across this statement. He stopped and he said, Man, he said, that is the foundation of Western civilization. And we ignore it at our peril. And I think he's perfectly right. So I see a responsibility as an academic and public intellectual, I suppose, to bring that in as a very serious philosophy and worldview and contrast it with the other worldviews that are unfortunately dominating still today, atheism, agnosticism, and all the rest of it. So there's that. But there's then the uniqueness of human beings goes further than simply a bland statement made in the image of God. And it's this, that we are unique in the following absolutely staggering sense. That human beings, model 101, if you like, like us, are the only kind of creature that God could become. Now that's a staggering statement because that's just putting what John says at the beginning of his gospel, the word, that is God, became flesh, became human. Now, when you reflect on that, that we are the sort of being that God could become, that is a powerful witness to my mind against this transhumanist attempt to create superhumans through artificial intelligence and all the rest of it. This is the bedrock, and this is what we need to explore. This universe is a word-based universe. By that I mean we can describe its physical nature to a certain extent in terms of mathematics, which is a language. It's word-based. Biology, one of the biggest discoveries of my lifetime, is the DNA code, which is the longest word we've ever discovered in a chemical language, 3.4 billion letters long is the human genome. It's a word-based living universe. And the statement in the beginning was the word resonates very deeply with me at all kinds of levels. So, why are we here? Well, the answer to that is as staggering as it is simple. You and I are here because God wanted us to be. Now, we need to think about that. In the book of Revelation, the last book of the Bible, about which I've just written another big, long book, there are various acts and scenes, a bit like a musical with themes that go through and reach a climax and then you start again. And one of them occurs in chapter 4 where there is praise in heaven for God as creator. But the actual wording is fascinating. It goes roughly like this. We praise you, O God, as creator because of your will they were and were created. Now, that's slightly awkward in contemporary English, but it's saying something absolutely staggering. You see, people are looking for meaning and purpose. And one of the dimensions of that is being accepted and loved, that there's someone who wants you to exist. And we all know if we've got kids and grandkids what it's like for a child to come home from school and say, Dad, they didn't want me. We can know that even as adults that they don't want us. And so I look at that statement of praise in heaven. I exist because God wanted me to be. That is utterly staggering. The government of the UK doesn't really know I exist. They want me to be a number in the IRS and so on. But this idea that there's a creator God who's not only vaguely interested, but to whom...

your existence is important. Now, that's just level one. That's the level of creation. But then this God becomes human to give us an even greater value because he's come to save us from the mess we've made of the world, our lives, and everything else. He's come to redeem us through Christ on the cross. And so we've got two levels of valuation. One is, I'm made in the image of God. God loves me whether I feel it or not. He wanted me to be. But now, in order to give me that well-being that you mentioned, that sense of living a good life, he's prepared to do something actively in my life. And that's hugely important. People often say to me, look, you're a scientist. You can't believe in this rubbish because you can't test it. I said, just a minute, you can test it. Jesus promised when he was on earth that people that turned away from the mess in life, their sin and rebellion, and we're all full of it, and trusted him as Lord and Savior, and that needs to be unpacked in detail, of course, they would experience certain things. First of all, they would experience peace. I meet many people who've no peace. They've no idea what peace is. I was interviewed on the famous Diary of a CEO recently. It was one of the biggest podcasts in the world and Stuart Barton. Millions have seen that, yes. Yes, he said, the peace you have and the confidence, I don't meet it in people other than Christians like you, which is a very encouraging thing from him to say. Not only peace, but a sense of forgiveness, and we need that. But above all, perhaps, it's the power that Christ gives if we follow him through his Spirit to not only have a sense of well-being, but to live a life that gives us that sense that is fulfilled and meaningful and purposeful. And you don't find it anywhere else. I often say, you know, when people say, but don't other religions and philosophies offer that? Well, none of them do, actually. And I put it this way, which is quite strong. I say, Jesus doesn't compete with anybody else, any other worldview, any other religion or philosophy, because he offers me something none of them do. Peace, forgiveness, certainty in this life, and then a certainty of being, if I use the technology word, uploaded, resurrected into a world to come where I will share with others who believe in him eternally the glories of a life that's utterly meaningful and full. So that's roughly speaking how I approach that. And I find that when talking to people, you can see that they know that they do not have it and they want it. But it involves certain steps of commitment, repentance, and sometimes they're not so prepared to do that. You have demonstrated peace in some very hostile situations, not just, say, communist countries, but in front of some people that were not very kind to you on the stage. You and I have both debated Christopher Hitchens, and I loved Christopher Hitchens, but he was pretty caustic in debates. And you, of course, have debated Peter Atkins, who's been very caustic in debates. And in your biography, friends, if you don't have John Lennox's biography, stop right now and purchase it, because you are going to be blessed by it. But you describe in this biography some different encounters you've had with people and how you've been able to disarm them with this peace that you have, John, even when they're unkind to you. How do you maintain that level of calm and composure in front of hostile audiences? Well, I think that I was pretty well prepared for it. In my youth, I saw a lot of hostility, both sectarian fighting and all this kind of thing in Northern Ireland. But I saw very rapidly that if you lose your cool, you've lost. And audiences recognize it. And so I observed very carefully the way in which Jesus talked to people. The only people he was angry with were religious bigots. But with other people, he was empathetic, sympathetic. He asked them questions. He listened to them, all this kind of thing. And I have proved in my life that a soft answer turns away wrath. And sometimes, even in public discussion forums, people will shift when they see that you're not hostile to them. You mentioned Christopher Hitchens. I liked him too. He was a showman, of course. And the aggressive stance and all the rest of it was part of the show. But I think one of the reasons I found it worthwhile debating these people in public was that the audience could see that I wasn't getting phased with this kind of thing, nor was I compromising what I believed. It's an exercise, in a way, in what Paul says in Ephesians, speaking truth in love. And you're right. You come, in a sense, deep down, to love these guys. You want to see them understanding the nature of the Christian message. And often, their pose and their attitude is because they've never understood it. It's quite clear they never have understood it. So it's important to keep doing it because people watch. And many people get converted even years later. I get letters from people who converted through watching my debate with Richard Dawkins. It started it all off. Yes. Yeah, at one point, Dawkins, during that debate, after you described the fact that God came into this universe, the Logos took on flesh and took our sins upon himself, he called that trivial. Oh, yes, it was more precisely what he did was, when I mentioned the resurrection, that was the point in that debate where we were suddenly told without warning that we got two minutes left each. And we were supposed to have finishing out the actual content of what was being asked at the time plus nine minutes each. And I'd spent months on those nine minutes. Suddenly told, for reasons that really were specious, that we'd only got two minutes. And I thought, what do I do with this? Because I had to go first. So I decided to go for the heart of Christianity, the resurrection, which is when he said, we've been talking all these great ideas and so on. And now we come down to the resurrection. How petty, how unworthy of the universe. Well, he was talking nonsense. If Jesus rose from the dead, it's one of the most significant things, if not the most significant thing that's ever happened. But that was a turning point for many people watching that. They saw the bankruptcy of his atheism that he had nothing. The emperor had no clothes. And therefore, I feel, as I look back, we were both quite upset by that robbing us of the proper way of finishing. But nevertheless, over the years, it's that that people refer to as the turning point in their lives. Now in the autobiography, you tell of a story when you were quite young and starting out about a Nobel laureate who kind of took you aside and said, Lennox, you got to drop this God thing. Can you relate that story? Well, he didn't quite take me aside, although in a sense he did. This was in my Cambridge college, my second year. So I was 19 or 20, maybe when it happened. And I just found myself sitting beside this man at dinner and did what I normally do with people, ask questions. And at one point, I asked him that when he did the work for which he won the Nobel Prize, did it ever occur to him that there might be an intelligence behind the universe? And he said, no, very sharply. And I could see he was being disingenuous. And that finished the conversation dead. He turned very pointedly to his neighbor, and I thought that's the end of it. But it wasn't the end of it. At the end of the meal, he essentially ordered me to come to his room, come to my room. So I went to his room. And he had two or three senior people from the university there. And my memory of it is that they sat me down and they stood and he said, now, do you want a career in science? And I said, yes, sir. Well, he said...

In front of witnesses here tonight, you give up this naive belief in God because if you pursue it, you will suffer by comparison with your peers. You'll never make it. So give it up. And I looked him straight in the eye. I can remember it so well. I said, Sir, tell me, what have you got to offer me that's better than what I've got in Christ? Just like that. And he said, Well, there's the evolutionary philosophy of Henri Bergson. Well, I knew what that was because I'd read C.S. Lewis and I didn't go into details. It was a very bad choice because Bergson himself talked about becoming a Catholic after the war. I said, If that's all you've got, I'll take the risk. I'll stick with Christ. And I got up and walked out. And that put a lot of steel into my heart and mind and it, I decided many things that day because it was a revelation of the unacceptable side of academia. And I resolved if I ever got into the kind of position I hold today, that I would never, ever consciously try and browbeat somebody. And I couldn't help reflecting that if he'd been a Christian and I'd been an atheist, he'd have lost his job the next day overdoing something like that. It was a terrible abuse of academic credentials. And I resolved that what I would do if I got the chance would be promote public discussion and give people the space to make up their own minds. And that's what I've done most of my life. And that comes from your parents' upbringing because your parents were that way. They wanted you to read. They wanted you... Didn't your father give you Das Kapital by Karl Marx? That's right. You've got a very good memory. And told me I needed to read it because I needed to know what other people thought. And they were humble people. He was not educated beyond 16. And yet he read voraciously and realized that it was very important for me to think not only about the Christian worldview but other worldviews. And I owe that to them. They opened scripture to me and it would never have occurred to me in those days that it was remotely boring because they made it fascinating and opened my mind. It was a mind opener, not a mind closer. So those were good preparations. But that incident has lived with me. It went very deep. And I'm glad it happened because it prepared me for the lesser minds of Dawkins and Hitchens and so on. And why would he need to browbeat you if he had all the evidence anyway? No, he has. Absolutely. I mean, when you begin to analyze it, it was almost incredible. And yet I've seen it. I have chatted to more than one Nobel Prize winner who's moved in that kind of direction. Well, I notice in the autobiography as well, toward the end of the autobiography, you talk about attending a university. I'm trying to remember where. But a Nobel laureate wanted you to send him your papers. It's in the autobiography, I think. Oh, yes, that is absolutely right. That happened at Texas A&M University where I was invited to give a lecture in the mathematics, physics department. Very prestigious. All sorts of... I remember that the head of department opened it up by saying, I don't want to put pressure on you, Professor Lennox, but we've got five National Academy members here and one Nobel Prize winner. And I talked, really, about why I think that science and faith in God can work very well together. And when I'd finished, the Nobel Prize winner started asking me questions. And he asked everybody to sit and wait. He said, have you written about this? I said, yes, sure. Well, he said, have you got anything here? And I gave him some script or something. Oh, no, he got me to write down a list of my books. So he kept everybody seated while he went out to the photocopier and made copies of these and gave them to everybody else. And then he came over to me and he said, I lost my wife last year and I'm beginning to think about things. Why have I never heard arguments like this before? These are entirely new to me. Staggering. Then you had another instance where you were sharing the stage with a woman who was a well-known atheist and she saw her husband decline and die. And you may have changed her worldview completely that night, John. I don't know where she is now, but... Well, that was... I've forgotten her surname, Margaret. And she is a world expert on assisted dying and all this kind of thing. And her husband had an awful cycle accident and she, in the end, had to allow the hospital to turn the life support off. And it was a Veritas forum in Utah State University. I'll never forget it. And I asked, could I meet her for a meal beforehand? Yes. I said, of course I would. So I stood up at the beginning. I said, look, this is a very unusual discussion on the problem of pain and suffering. silence and it's a Veritas forum talk.
